ohio-facts-state-symbols.title: Ohio Facts: State Symbols
ohio-facts-state-symbols.body_html:
Since the early 1800s, Ohio lawmakers have chosen symbols to honor the state’s people, places, and history. Most of these symbols are listed in Chapter 5 of the Ohio Revised Code, while others were created through special resolutions passed by the legislature.

State Flag

Ohio’s state flag is called the Ohio burgee. It was designed by John Eisenmann in 1901 and became the official state flag in 1902. Unlike most state flags, it has a swallowtail shape, which makes it unique.

The flag has:

  • Five stripes (three red and two white) for Ohio’s roads and rivers,
  • A blue triangle that stands for the state’s hills and valleys.
  • Seventeen white stars to show that Ohio was the 17th state to join the U.S., and
  • A red circle with a white border in the center, which looks like an “O” for Ohio and also represents the state’s nickname, the Buckeye State.

The flag’s design is described in Ohio Revised Code, Section 5.01. Rules for displaying and caring for the flag are in Ohio Revised Code, Section 5.012.

Coat of Arms and State Seal

Ohio’s coat of arms shows a sunrise over Mount Logan, with the Scioto River and a farm field in the foreground. On the left is a sheaf of wheat, and on the right is a bundle of 17 arrows, representing Ohio as the 17th state. The design is described in Ohio Revised Code, Section 5.04.

The Great Seal of the State of Ohio includes the coat of arms inside a circle with the words “THE GREAT SEAL OF THE STATE OF OHIO.” The current design was adopted in 1996. The seal is used by state officials, courts, and some agencies. Others must get permission from the Governor’s Office to use it. Rules for the seal’s design and use are in Ohio Revised Code, section 5.10.

State Motto

Ohio’s state motto is “With God, All Things Are Possible.” It was suggested in 1958 by James Mastronardo, a 10-year-old from Cincinnati. With help from his state senator, he gathered signatures and spoke to lawmakers to support the idea. The motto became official in October 1959. 

The phrase, a favorite of his mother, is from the Bible—Matthew 19:26. While it comes from a religious text, it’s meant to express hope and determination, not to promote a specific religion.

The motto is defined in Ohio Revised Code, section 5.06.

State Slogan

Ohio’s official slogan is “Ohio, The Heart of it All.” It highlights Ohio’s central location and its strong sense of community. The slogan is used to promote tourism and to show that Ohio is a great place to live, learn, work, and raise a family.

State agencies and organizations also use the slogan to share what makes Ohio special. It’s part of the state’s official branding for visitors and residents alike

State Capital and Capitol Building

Columbus is Ohio’s capital city. It's located in Franklin county, near the center of the state.

The Ohio Statehouse, found in downtown Columbus, is where the state’s government meets. It has:

  • A large rotunda (a round, domed room),
  • Meeting rooms and chambers for the Ohio Senate and House of Representatives,
  • The Senate Building, which holds more offices and hearing rooms,
  • A big atrium used for public events and rentals, and
  • A gift shop for visitors.

The Statehouse is not just a government building—it’s also a historic site and a symbol of Ohio’s democracy.

State Nickname

Ohio is known as the Buckeye state. People from Ohio are often called Buckeyes, a nickname that dates back to the early 1800s. The name comes from the buckeye tree, which grows across the state. Its nut looks like a deer’s eye—dark brown with a light spot—and early settlers thought it was a good symbol for Ohio.

The nickname became popular during William Henry Harrison’s presidential campaign in 1840. His supporters made souvenirs from buckeye wood, helping the name stick.

Today, “Buckeye” is used all over Ohio. For example, you'll find it:

  • In place names like Buckeye Lake and the Buckeye Trail,
  • In the names of many businesses and organizations, and
  • As the official mascot of The Ohio State University.

What started as a simple nickname is now a proud symbol of Ohio’s identity.

State-Declared Holidays and Observances

The Ohio Legislature can create special days, weeks, or months to raise awareness about important people, events, or causes. These observances are listed in Chapter 5 of the Ohio Revised Code, along with the state’s official symbols.

Some examples include:

  • Ohio Statehood Day
  • Breast Cancer Awareness Month
  • Veterans’ Day
  • Ohio Overdose Awareness Day

These observances help educate the public and honor Ohio’s history, health, and community.

State Animals

Bird: Cardinal

Adopted: 1953

The cardinal is Ohio’s official state bird. It’s a small songbird that stays in Ohio all year.

Cardinals are easy to spot:

  • Males are bright red with a black mask around their faces.
  • Females are brownish-gray with red-orange highlights on their wings, tails, and crests.
  • Both have a sharp crest of feathers on their heads and a bright orange beak.

Cardinals eat seeds, fruits, and insects. They are known for being territorial and often mate for life.

The state bird is defined in Ohio Revised Code, section 5.06.

Insect: Ladybug

Adopted: 1975

The ladybug, also called the ladybird beetle, is Ohio’s official state insect. It’s a small, shiny red bug with black spots, active from spring through fall.

Ladybugs are harmless to people but very helpful to farmers and gardeners. They eat aphids and other bugs that damage plants.

The most common type in Ohio is the seven-spotted ladybug. It has:

  • A red body,
  • Three black spots on each side, and
  • One black spot in the middle.

Their bright colors and bad taste help protect them from predators.

Mammal: White-Tailed Deer

Adopted: 1988

The white-tailed deer has lived in Ohio since the last Ice Age. It has a gray-brown coat and gets its name from the white underside of its tail, which it raises when alarmed.

Native peoples used deer for food, clothing, and tools. Early settlers traded deerskins for supplies, which is how the word “buck” came to mean money.

White-tailed deer are foragers. They eat grasses, nuts, berries, wildflowers, crops, and woody plants. Because of their diet, they’re often found near forests and neighborhoods

Reptile: Black Racer Snake

Adopted: 1995

The black racer lives mostly in the eastern and southern parts of the state.

This snake is:

  • Solid black with no markings,
  • Usually 3 to 5 feet long, and
  • Known for being very fast—it can move up to 10 miles per hour!

Black racers are helpful to farmers and gardeners because they eat rodents and other small pests. While they can act aggressive if they feel threatened, their bite is not poisonous—just painful.

Amphibian: Spotted Salamander

Adopted: 2010

The spotted salamander lives in moist woodlands near ponds, swamps, and creeks.

These salamanders are:

  • Nocturnal (active at night),
  • Shy burrowers that spend most of their time underground,
  • About 6 to 7.75 inches long, and
  • Able to live up to 20 years.

They eat insects, earthworms, small amphibians, and even tiny mice. Because they’re hard to spot, seeing one in the wild is a special treat!

Frog: American Bullfrog

Adopted: 2010

The bullfrog is the largest frog in North America. It lives in ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams across the state.

Bullfrogs are:

  • Green with brown markings,
  • About 3.5 to 6 inches long, and
  • Known for their deep, loud call, which can be heard up to a mile away!

They are solitary and territorial. They eat crayfish, insects, mice, and even other frogs. Bullfrogs can live for 7 to 9 years and are most active from late April through summer.

Pet: Shelter Pet

Adopted: 2019

Ohio named the shelter pet as its official state pet to help raise awareness about the many cats and dogs waiting for homes in shelters across the state.

Each year, about 6.5 million animals enter shelters in the U.S., but only half are adopted. By choosing a shelter pet, you’re giving an animal a second chance at life.

To adopt, contact your local animal shelter or humane society and learn how you can help a pet find a loving home.

State Plant Life

Flower: Red Carnation

Adopted: 1953

The scarlet carnation is a colorful plant with fringed petals and a spicy scent. The flower is popular in bouquets and can grow up to 2.5 feet tall.

The red carnation stands for love and passion. It was a favorite of President William McKinley, who was born in Ohio and often wore one on his jacket. 

Tree: Ohio Buckeye

Adopted: 1953

The buckeye tree is native to North America. In late summer and early fall, it produces a nut that’s dark brown with a light spot, resembling a deer’s eye—which is how the tree got its name.

The nut also inspired the popular chocolate buckeye candy. These treats are made of peanut butter dipped in chocolate, with a bit of the lighter-colored filling left showing to look like the real nut. While the buckeye nut is poisonous, the candy version is safe and delicious

Wild Flower: White Trillium

Adopted: 1987

The white trillium grows in all 88 Ohio counties and blooms in the spring with a large, white flower made of three petals.

Also called the wake robin or snow trillium, this plant grows best in shady woodlands. Native Americans once used its leaves for food and roots for medicine.

Fruit: Tomato

Adopted: 2009

Many experts credit Alexander W. Livingston, an Ohio native, with creating the modern tomato. In 1870, he developed the “Paragon” tomato, which was larger and sweeter than most tomatoes at the time.

Livingston went on to grow tomatoes commercially and created more than 30 varieties. By the late 1800s, tomato farming had become a big part of Ohio’s agriculture—and it still is today.

Native Fruit: Pawpaw

Adopted: 2009

The pawpaw is the only edible fruit native to Ohio. Native Americans in the Ohio Valley used it for food and trade as early as the 1500s.

Pawpaws are:

  • 2 to 4 inches long,
  • Green, yellow, or brown, depending on how ripe they are, and
  • Shaped like a short, fat banana.

They taste like a mix of banana and mango and are packed with protein, vitamin C, iron, and potassium. The best time to pick pawpaws is in mid-September.

Human-Made State Symbols

Beverage: Tomato Juice

Adopted: 1965

In 1870, Ohioan Alexander W. Livingston created the modern tomato with his sweet and juicy “Paragon” variety. His tomatoes helped make tomato juice a popular and healthy drink.

Tomato juice is:

  • Rich in antioxidants and electrolytes,
  • Lower in sugar than many fruit juices, and
  • Great in soups, sauces, or as a refreshing drink.

Due to its popularity, tomatoes and tomato juice are big parts of Ohio’s farming and food industry.

Song: "Beautiful Ohio"

Adopted: 1989

The music for “Beautiful Ohio” was written by Mary Earl, and the original lyrics were by Ballard MacDonald. In 1989, Wilbert B. McBride updated the lyrics to better reflect Ohio’s cities, industries, and farmland.

The song celebrates Ohio’s beauty and strength. Here’s the chorus:

Beautiful Ohio, where the golden grain
Dwarfs the lovely flowers in the summer rain.
Cities rising high, silhouette the sky.
Freedom is supreme in this majestic land;
Mighty factories seem to hum in tune, so grand.
Beautiful Ohio, thy wonders are in view,
Land where my dreams all come true!

Rock Song: "Hang On Sloopy

Adopted: 1985

Ohio is the only state with an official rock song—“Hang on Sloopy.” It became a hit in 1965 when it was recorded by The McCoys, a band with Ohio roots. Two members, Randy and Rick Derringer, were from the state.

The song is believed to be about Dorothy Sloop, a singer from Steubenville, Ohio, who used the nickname Sloopy.

The Ohio State University Marching Band first played the song at a football game in October 1965. The version arranged by John Tagenhorst became a fan favorite and is still played at games today. It’s now a proud part of Ohio’s music and sports culture.

Bicentennial Bridge: Blaine Hill Bridge

Adopted: 2002

The Blaine Hill Bridge is the oldest and longest sandstone bridge in Ohio. It was built in 1826 and crosses Wheeling Creek in Belmont County.

The bridge has a unique three-arch “S” shape and was part of the National Road Project, which helped connect the country in the 1800s. It closed to traffic in 1994, but local efforts saved it from being torn down.

In 1999, the Blaine Bridge Community Preservation Project began restoring the bridge. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2010.

Prehistoric Monument: Newark Earthworks

Adopted: 2006

Long ago, ancient people in what is now Ohio built huge shapes and structures out of earth. These were made by the Hopewell culture between 1 and 400 A.D.

The Newark Earthworks is the largest of these sites. It once covered over 4 square miles and used more than 7 million cubic feet of soil. The site was likely used as a ceremonial center, a burial ground, and even an astronomical observatory.

Today, three major parts of the earthworks still remain:

  • The Great Circle, which includes Eagle Mound,
  • The Octagon Earthworks, which align with the moon’s movements, and
  • The Wright Earthworks, a smaller section that shows how the site once looked.

These earthworks are a powerful reminder of Ohio’s ancient history and are now protected as a World Heritage Site.

Artifact: Adena Pipe

Adopted: 2013

The Adena Pipe is one of Ohio’s most famous ancient artifacts. It was found in 1901 in a burial mound near Chillicothe, on the estate of Thomas Worthington, Ohio’s 6th governor.

The pipe is carved from Ohio pipestone and shaped like a man wearing a loincloth and feather bustle. It was likely used for ceremonial tobacco smoking and may have belonged to a leader or spiritual figure.

The Adena culture, which built the mound, lived in the Scioto and Hocking River valleys from about 800 B.C. to 100 A.D. 

Historical Architectural Structure: Barn

Adopted: 2019

Barns are a big part of Ohio’s farming history. You can find them all over the state—from Lake Erie to the Ohio River. These buildings come in many shapes, sizes, and colors, depending on the needs of the farm and the style of the builder.

Some barns were even painted with murals or ads. From 1997 to 2002, artist Scott Hagan painted a barn in each of Ohio’s 88 counties with a special logo to celebrate Ohio’s 200th birthday in 2003.

Barns remind us of Ohio’s strong agricultural roots and the people who helped build its communities.

Airplane: 1905 Wright Flyer III

Adopted: 2025

In 1905, Ohio inventors Wilbur and Orville Wright built the Wright Flyer III. It was their strongest and most reliable airplane yet.

On June 23, 1905, Orville Wright made the first flight with it. By October, the plane flew 25 miles—a huge improvement over earlier flights. It was also the first airplane to carry a passenger, marking a major moment in aviation history.

Geological Symbols

Gemstone: Flint

Adopted: 1965

Flint is a tough, glassy rock that was very important to Native Americans in Ohio. A type of quartz, it breaks into sharp edges, making it perfect for tools and weapons.Early settlers also used it for starting fires, flintlock guns, and grinding tools. 

The best source in the state was Flint Ridge, located in Licking and Muskingum counties. People came from hundreds of miles away to gather flint there. 

Today, flint is often polished and worn as jewelry.

Fossil: Isotelus

Adopted: 1985

Isotelus was trilobite. a sea animal with a hard shell and no backbone. The name “trilobite” means “three-lobed,” because their bodies looked like they were divided into three parts.

Isotelus was one of the biggest trilobites ever found—some grew over two feet long! These animals went extinct about 430 million years ago, but their fossils are still found in Ohio. They show that this area was once covered by a shallow sea.

Fossil Fish: Dunkleosteus Terrelli (a.k.a., "the Dunk")

Adopted: 2021

Dunkleosteus terrelli lived long before the dinosaurs and was a top predator of the sea that once covered Ohio.

Nicknamed the "Dunk," this placoderm had thick, bony plates covering its head and body. Dunks grew up to 29 feet long and could weigh more than 4 tons—bigger than a modern great white shark! Though they had no teeth, Dunks had strong jaws that could crush or slice its prey.

The Dunk went extinct about 360 million years ago, but fossils have been found in Ohio’s shale rocks. You can see many of them on display at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History.

ohio-facts-geography.title: Ohio Facts: Geography
ohio-facts-geography.body_html:
Location and Size

Ohio is in the Midwest and covers about 44,825 square miles. It borders:

  • North: Michigan and Lake Erie
  • East: Pennsylvania
  • Southeast: West Virginia
  • South: Kentucky
  • West: Indiana

The center point of the state is Centerburg in Knox County. Other extreme points include:

  • Northernmost: Conneaut, Ashtabula County
  • Southernmost: Burlington, Lawrence County
  • Easternmost: Masury, Trumbull County
  • Westernmost: Elizabethtown, Hamilton County

Time zone: Eastern Time (with Daylight Saving Time from March to November)

Elevation

  • Average elevation: 850 feet
  • Highest point: Campbell Hill (1,550 feet)
  • Lowest point: Ohio River in the southwest (455 feet)

Land Features

Ohio is mostly flat with some hills, valleys, and beaches. The Till Plains cover the west, while the Appalachian Plateau shapes the east. In the south, you’ll find caves, cliffs, and rock formations.

Ohio is rich in natural resources, with over 50 types of minerals, including quartz, flint, salt, gold, and gypsum.

The state also produces large amounts of rock used in construction and manufacturing, including coal, clay, limestone, and gravel.

Waterways

Ohio has more than 3,300 rivers and streams and 60,000 lakes and ponds.

  • Lake Erie forms the northern border
  • The Ohio River runs along the south and southeast

Major lakes: Pymatuning, Grand Lake, Mosquito Creek
Major rivers: Scioto, Muskingum, Cuyahoga, Maumee, Hocking, Olentangy, and more

Weather and Climate

Ohio has four seasons, with weather that is typical for the American Midwest.

  • Summers are usually hot and humid, while winters are cold and wet.
  • Many plants and trees bloom in the spring and go dormant in the fall.

Severe weather can include:

  • Thunderstorms and tornadoes (summer)
  • Snow and ice (winter)
  • Flooding (any time of year)

Average July high temperature: 85.3°F
Average January low temperature: 36.2°F
Average yearly rainfall: 37.57 inches

ohio-facts-plants-animals.title: Ohio Facts: Plants and Animals
ohio-facts-plants-animals.body_html:
Animals

Ohio is home to hundreds of animal species, including:

  • Mammals: deer, squirrels, raccoons, and black bears
  • Reptiles & Amphibians: snakes and frogs
  • Marine Life: fish, mollusks, and crustaceans
  • Birds: from songbirds to hawks

You'll also find more than 1,000 species of insects, including ants, flies, bees, beetles, butterflies, moths, grasshoppers, and dragonflies

Trees

More than 120 types of trees grow in Ohio. Most are broad-leaf trees that lose their leaves in fall and grow them back in spring.

Common types include:

  • Hardwoods: oaks, maples, elms, hickories, and dogwoods
  • Fruit trees: apple and cherry
  • Evergreens: pine, spruce, and fir

Plants

Ohio has more than 300,000 plant species, including:

  • Flowering plants: sunflowers, violets, asters, trilliums, goldenrods, irises, azaleas, and orchids
  • Non-flowering plants: mosses and ferns

Fruits and Vegetables

Thanks to warm summers and mild seasons, Ohio grows a wide variety of crops, including:

  • Grains: corn and wheat
  • Vegetables: carrots, cabbage, lettuce, onions, peas, beans, radishes, tomatoes, peppers, and pumpkins
  • Fruits: grapes, apples, cherries, and berries

ohio-facts-entertainment-sports-leisure.title: Ohio Facts: Entertainment, Sports, and Leisure
ohio-facts-entertainment-sports-leisure.body_html:
These are some of the biggest entertainment sources in Ohio. Visit Ohio.org to learn about the many things to do and places to visit in Ohio.

Amusement Parks

Ohio is home to two top-tier theme parks—Cedar Point in Sandusky and Kings Island in Mason. Both are known for thrilling roller coasters and family fun.

Along with these major parks, Ohio also has more than a dozen smaller amusement parks that locals love. Plus, you’ll find indoor and outdoor waterparks across the state, perfect for year-round fun.

Collegiate Sports

With over 50 colleges and universities, Ohio is a powerhouse in college sports. Schools across the state compete in six NCAA Division I conferences:

  • Atlantic 10: Dayton Flyers
  • Big East: Xavier Musketeers
  • Big Ten: Ohio State Buckeyes
  • Big Twelve: Cincinnati Bearcats
  • Horizon League: Cleveland State Vikings, Wright State Raiders
  • Mid-American Conference: Akron Zips, Bowling Green Falcons, Kent State Golden Flashes, Miami Redhawks, Ohio University Bobcats, and Toledo Rockets

Many other Ohio schools compete in NCAA Divisions II and III, as well as in the NAIA, NJCAA, Ohio Regional Campus Conference, and USCAA. Sports include football, basketball, baseball, softball, ice hockey, and soccer.

Museums and Learning Experiences

Ohio’s museums bring art, history, and science to life. From local stories to world-class art, from aviation to industry, you can explore it all in fun and creative ways.

Whether large or small, these museums offer something for everyone.

National and State Parks

Ohio is rich in natural beauty and history. The state has 8 National Parks, 2 National Trails, 23 National Natural Landmarks, and 76 National Historic Landmarks. More than 4,000 places in Ohio are listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Ohio’s State Park System includes more than 70 parks and 1,000 miles of trails. Visitors can enjoy hiking, boating, swimming, fishing, hunting, camping, golf, lodges, and more—year-round.

Professional Sports

Ohio hosts teams in all five major professional sports leagues, including:

  • Major League Baseball (MLB): Cincinnati Reds and Cleveland Guardians.
  • Major League Soccer (MLS): Columbus Crew and FC Cincinnati
  • National Basketball Association (NBA): Cleveland Cavaliers
  • National Football League (NFL): Cincinnati Bengals and Cleveland Browns.
  • National Hockey League (NHL): Columbus Blue Jackets.

Ohio also has many minor league teams in baseball, football, basketball, hockey, and soccer.

The state is home to iconic sports venues that host major games and global events.They include:

  • Great American Ball Park and Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati,
  • Progressive Field and Cleveland Browns Stadium in Cleveland, and
  • Ohio Stadium, Nationwide Arena, and Lower.com Field in Columbus.

Inverness Club (Toledo) and Muirfield Village (Dublin) host PGA events, while Highland Meadows (Sylvania) and Kenwood Country Club (Cincinnati) host LPGA tournaments.

NASCAR and IndyCar races take place at Mid-Ohio Sports Car Course, and NHRA drag races are held at Summit Motorsports Park.

Ohio’s football legacy runs deep. The Pro Football Hall of Fame is in Canton, and every NFL game ball is made at the Wilson Football Factory in Ada.

Zoos and Wildlife

Ohio is a great place to explore and learn about wildlife. The Toledo Zoo, Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, and Columbus Zoo are ranked among the best in the country.

Across the state, you’ll also find aquariums, safari parks, bird sanctuaries, and smaller zoos that offer up-close animal experiences for all ages.
